articles.title: Nearly 3,000 exploding stars challenge our understanding of the Universe
articles.summary: A massive analysis of 2,884 exploding stars has uncovered new evidence that dark energy, the mysterious force accelerating the universe’s expansion, may change over time. The findings challenge a cornerstone of modern cosmology and could reshape our understanding of how the universe works.
articles.content:
The largest collection of exploding white dwarf stars ever compiled is providing fresh evidence that dark energy, the mysterious force responsible for the Universe’s accelerating expansion, may change over time. The findings challenge a central assumption of modern cosmology and could help scientists better understand how the Universe evolves.

An international research team led by scientists at the University of Queensland’s School of Mathematics and Physics brought together observations of 2,884 Type Ia supernovae. These powerful stellar explosions serve as important tools for measuring distances across the Universe, allowing astronomers to trace its expansion history.

PhD candidate Ryan Camilleri said the project establishes a new international standard for supernova cosmology. By bringing decades of measurements into a unified dataset, researchers have created their most detailed picture yet of how cosmic expansion has changed over time.

“We’ve rebuilt 3 decades of astronomical observations into a single, consistent framework,” Mr. Camilleri said.

“We combined our data with other cosmic measurements including relic light from the Big Bang and maps of how galaxies are distributed through space.

“Instead of confirming the standard model of cosmology which assumes dark energy is fixed and unchanging, we have more evidence that dark energy may change over time.”

Combining Three Decades of Supernova Observations

The new collection brings together historical supernova measurements and findings from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) published in 2024.

To make observations collected over different periods directly comparable, the scientists revisited older data using updated analytical methods. Advances in understanding supernova behavior allowed the team to improve the consistency and accuracy of measurements gathered over decades.

“Over the years we’ve learned a lot more about how supernovae behave so we’ve been able to go back and apply that improved understanding to older data,” Mr. Camilleri said.

The researchers also had to account for differences among the telescopes used to collect the observations. Other factors, including cosmic dust and the masses of galaxies, can influence the light astronomers receive from distant supernovae and therefore affect distance measurements.

“Extensive work has been done to link observations from different telescopes with different capacities and take into account issues such as cosmic dust and galaxy mass which can affect the light coming from a supernova.

“We also incorporated more subtle effects such as gravitational lensing, which is the bending and magnification of light around large objects as it travels from a supernova to Earth.”

New Evidence Challenges the Dark Energy Model

Astrophysicist Professor Tamara Davis said the expanded dataset represents an important advance in efforts to understand the nature of dark energy.

Under the standard model of cosmology, dark energy is treated as a constant property of the Universe. However, recent observations have raised questions about whether that assumption fully explains how cosmic expansion has evolved.

“Our supernova data from DES in 2024 first showed hints that dark energy may be time varying, and this new compilation also sees a deviation from the standard model although in a slightly different direction,” Professor Davis said.

The findings are especially interesting because a separate astronomical project has also produced evidence suggesting that dark energy might not remain constant.

“Similarly results from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) found hints of variations in dark energy in its surveys of relic sound waves from the early Universe.

“So, 2 completely independent measurements have found hints of time variation in dark energy, challenging the standard model that dark energy doesn't change.

Although the different measurements do not point to exactly the same departure from the standard model, they provide additional reasons to investigate whether dark energy changes as the Universe ages.

Could Dark Energy Help Unite Gravity and Quantum Physics?

Understanding dark energy could have implications extending far beyond the expansion of the Universe. Researchers believe that learning more about its behavior might also provide insights into one of the greatest unresolved problems in theoretical physics: reconciling gravity with quantum physics.

“All of this research may also hold the clue to explain how gravity and quantum physics fit together.

“We know these 2 theories are each immensely successful in their own realms, so if we can figure out how to put them together that would be a huge step in theoretical physics.”

Future Supernova Surveys Could Provide More Answers

The researchers plan to expand the dataset as additional observations become available. One important source will be the Dark Energy Bedrock All-Sky Supernova program (DEBASS), which is identifying hundreds of supernovae at distances closer to Earth than those surveyed by DES.

Incorporating these nearby explosions will provide further measurements that scientists can use to investigate the Universe’s expansion and test whether dark energy truly changes over time.

The cosmology findings are available on arXiv here, while the accompanying measurements of host galaxy masses can be found on arXiv here.

International Collaboration Behind the Research

The new results build on decades of work by hundreds of astronomers and researchers worldwide. Contributing projects include the Dark Energy Survey, Foundation Supernova Survey, PanStarrs I, Sloan Digital Sky Survey, Supernova Legacy Survey, Carnegie Supernova Project, and the Center for Astrophysics supernova survey.

articles.personality_title: Thousands of exploding stars reveal new clues about dark energy
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists study exploding stars called Type Ia supernovae to measure how the Universe expands. These stars act like cosmic markers because their brightness helps calculate distances in space.

**What happened** – An international team led by the University of Queensland combined data from 2,884 supernovae observed over 30 years. They used new methods to make old and new data consistent, including recent findings from the Dark Energy Survey in 2024. This large dataset gave a clearer picture of how the Universe’s expansion may have changed over time.

**Impact** – Their analysis suggests that dark energy, the mysterious force pushing the Universe to expand faster, might not be constant as previously thought. This challenges a key idea in modern cosmology. Independent studies, like the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, also hint at changes in dark energy, supporting this new view.

**What's next step** – Researchers will add more supernova data from upcoming surveys like the Dark Energy Bedrock All-Sky Supernova program. These new observations will test if dark energy really changes, improving our understanding of cosmic expansion and possibly helping unite gravity with quantum physics.

**One-sentence takeaway** – By studying nearly 3,000 exploding stars, scientists found new evidence that dark energy may change over time, challenging existing ideas about the Universe’s growth.

articles.personality_title_es: Casi 3.000 estrellas en explosión revelan nuevas pistas sobre la energía oscura
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos estudian estrellas que explotan llamadas supernovas tipo Ia para medir cómo se expande el Universo. La luz de estas estrellas ayuda a calcular distancias en el espacio.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo internacional liderado por la Universidad de Queensland reunió datos de 2.884 supernovas observadas durante 30 años. Usaron nuevos métodos para hacer que los datos antiguos y recientes fueran comparables, incluyendo hallazgos de la Encuesta de Energía Oscura de 2024. Este gran conjunto de datos mostró una imagen más clara de cómo podría haber cambiado la expansión del Universo.

**Impacto** – Su análisis sugiere que la energía oscura, la fuerza misteriosa que acelera la expansión del Universo, podría no ser constante como se creía. Esto desafía una idea clave de la cosmología moderna. Estudios independientes, como el Instrumento Espectroscópico de Energía Oscura, también muestran indicios de cambios en la energía oscura.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores añadirán más datos de supernovas de futuras encuestas como el programa Dark Energy Bedrock All-Sky Supernova. Estas nuevas observaciones ayudarán a comprobar si la energía oscura realmente cambia, mejorando nuestra comprensión de la expansión cósmica y posiblemente ayudando a unir la gravedad con la física cuántica.

**Resumen en una frase** – Al estudiar casi 3.000 estrellas en explosión, los científicos encontraron nuevas pruebas de que la energía oscura podría cambiar con el tiempo, cuestionando las ideas actuales sobre el crecimiento del Universo.

articles.title: Tiny ‘solar flares’ recreated in the lab may explain corona mystery
articles.summary: An experiment has produced nanoflares similar to those seen on the sun, and shown that they can help explain why the outer layers of the solar atmosphere are so hot
articles.content:
An experiment has produced nanoflares similar to those seen on the sun, and shown that they can help explain why the outer layers of the solar atmosphere are so hot

Activity on the sun, as captured by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory NASA/SDO/AIA

With powerful lasers and a tiny piece of plastic, researchers have for the first time emulated a violent process that may take place on the sun. The experiment could help shed light on why the outermost layer of the sun’s atmosphere is so mysteriously hot.

For decades, scientists have struggled to explain why the sun’s outer atmospheric layers – a region called the corona – are thousands of times hotter than the sun’s surface, reaching several millions of degrees. “It is as if the air grew hotter as you walked away from a campfire,” says Wei Sun at the China Institute of Atomic Energy.

Now, Sun and his colleagues have emulated some of the conditions on the sun in the lab and, for the first time, observed how tiny bursts of electromagnetic radiation, or solar nanoflares, could power the corona’s puzzling heat.

Advertisement

Nanoflares are known to occur when magnetic fields within the corona abruptly rearrange themselves and emit energy in the process. But for this rearrangement to happen, the exact conditions, such as the shape of the magnetic fields, must be just right, says Sun. He and his colleagues investigated how these conditions could arise and ultimately lead to nanoflares. They fired four very powerful lasers onto a tiny plastic target, which produced a patch of plasma – a hot mixture of charged particles – about 2 millimetres across. This plasma was not an exact recreation of plasma in the sun’s corona but behaved analogously.

The team created plasmas in two different scenarios, once using a flat target and once using one with a wavy surface. In the second case, the plasma became unstable and the magnetic fields it contained rearranged themselves and ultimately produced a nanoflare.

This nanoflare made a big difference to the temperature of the plasma. It reached temperatures of 799,726°C, which was nearly double the temperature achieved in the flat target version of the experiment where no nanoflares occurred.

A similar process – instability leading to nanoflares leading to plasma heating – could feasibly happen on the sun, says Sun. In fact, the parameters that determined their tiny plasma’s behaviour matched those observed in regions of the sun where blobs of colder plasma “rain” down through the corona. He and his colleagues also completed a computer simulation that corroborated this.

Rony Keppens at KU Leuven in Belgium says that these simulations support the team’s interpretation of the experiment and make for an interesting entry on to the list of effects that may be contributing to coronal heating. Coronal rain blobs really could lead to the kinds of instabilities that the researchers now spotted in the lab, he says. Yet, in Keppens’s view, the new experiment does not definitively resolve the coronal heating puzzle, as other plasma behaviours, such as certain types of waves in it, could also contribute to it.

Going forward, Sun and his colleagues want to upgrade their experiment to create more three-dimensional plasmas and use more precise techniques for diagnosing its behaviour. And they want to make their laboratory measurements more directly comparable to reality – for example, by using data about the sun collected through telescopes, says Sun. “It is important to check that the laboratory is reproducing what the sun does,” he says.

This discovery has broad implications for understanding solar physics, which affects space weather and ultimately life on Earth. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights a meaningful advancement in space science.
articles.personality_title: Scientists recreate tiny solar flares in lab to explain sun’s hot outer atmosphere
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long wondered why the sun’s outer atmosphere, called the corona, is much hotter than its surface. The corona can reach millions of degrees, while the surface is much cooler. This mystery has puzzled researchers for decades.

**What happened** – Researchers used powerful lasers and a small plastic target to create tiny bursts of energy called nanoflares in a laboratory. These nanoflares acted like those on the sun and showed how magnetic fields can suddenly change and release energy. The experiment heated plasma to nearly 800,000°C, almost twice as hot as plasma without nanoflares.

**Impact** – This lab experiment helps explain how nanoflares could heat the sun’s corona. It shows that certain magnetic field shapes can cause energy bursts that raise temperatures. This is an important step in understanding solar activity, which affects space weather and technology on Earth.

**What's next step** – The team plans to improve their experiment by creating more realistic plasma and comparing their results with real data from solar telescopes. This will help confirm if their lab findings match what happens on the sun.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have recreated tiny solar flares in the lab, providing new clues about why the sun’s outer atmosphere is so hot.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des chercheurs recréent de minuscules éruptions solaires en laboratoire pour expliquer la chaleur de la couronne solaire
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques se demandent depuis longtemps pourquoi la couche extérieure du soleil, appelée la couronne, est beaucoup plus chaude que sa surface. La couronne peut atteindre des millions de degrés, alors que la surface est beaucoup plus froide. Ce mystère intrigue les chercheurs depuis des décennies.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs ont utilisé des lasers puissants et une petite cible en plastique pour créer en laboratoire de minuscules explosions d’énergie appelées nanoflares. Ces nanoflares ressemblent à ceux du soleil et montrent comment les champs magnétiques peuvent soudainement changer et libérer de l’énergie. L’expérience a chauffé un plasma à près de 800 000°C, presque deux fois plus chaud que le plasma sans nanoflares.

**Impact** – Cette expérience en laboratoire aide à expliquer comment les nanoflares pourraient chauffer la couronne solaire. Elle montre que certaines formes des champs magnétiques peuvent provoquer des explosions d’énergie qui augmentent la température. C’est une avancée importante pour comprendre l’activité solaire, qui influence la météo spatiale et la technologie sur Terre.

**Étape suivante** – L’équipe prévoit d’améliorer son expérience en créant un plasma plus réaliste et en comparant ses résultats avec des données réelles provenant de télescopes solaires. Cela permettra de vérifier si leurs découvertes en laboratoire correspondent à ce qui se passe sur le soleil.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Des scientifiques ont recréé en laboratoire de minuscules éruptions solaires, apportant de nouveaux indices pour comprendre pourquoi la couche extérieure du soleil est si chaude.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos recrean pequeñas erupciones solares en laboratorio para explicar el calor de la atmósfera solar
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante mucho tiempo, los científicos se han preguntado por qué la capa exterior del sol, llamada corona, es mucho más caliente que su superficie. La corona puede alcanzar millones de grados, mientras que la superficie es mucho más fría. Este misterio ha desconcertado a los investigadores durante décadas.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores usaron láseres potentes y un pequeño objetivo de plástico para crear en el laboratorio pequeñas explosiones de energía llamadas nanoflares. Estos nanoflares son similares a los que ocurren en el sol y muestran cómo los campos magnéticos pueden cambiar de repente y liberar energía. El experimento calentó un plasma a casi 800,000°C, casi el doble que el plasma sin nanoflares.

**Impacto** – Este experimento de laboratorio ayuda a explicar cómo los nanoflares podrían calentar la corona solar. Demuestra que ciertas formas de campos magnéticos pueden causar explosiones de energía que aumentan la temperatura. Esto es un paso importante para entender la actividad solar, que afecta el clima espacial y la tecnología en la Tierra.

**Próximo paso** – El equipo planea mejorar su experimento creando plasmas más realistas y comparando sus resultados con datos reales obtenidos de telescopios solares. Esto ayudará a confirmar si sus hallazgos en el laboratorio coinciden con lo que ocurre en el sol.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Científicos han recreado pequeñas erupciones solares en laboratorio, aportando nuevas pistas sobre por qué la atmósfera exterior del sol es tan caliente.
